runs.t: This manual replaces Chapter 8 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (2020), book pages 219 to 250. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objectives, and marks every place where this document differs from the book, so you always know what is from the book and what is not.

Read it top to bottom: pre-check, sections 8.1 to 8.4, troubleshooting, labs, review questions, then the revision sheet and tracker table. Nothing here was run on real Cisco equipment. Where a command or output was not run, it is marked

2.0 Network Access (v1.0 numbering used by the book)
2.1 Configure and verify VLANs (normal range) spanning multiple switches: 2.1.a Access ports (data and voice); 2.1.b Default VLAN; 2.1.c Connectivity.
2.2 Configure and verify interswitch connectivity: 2.2.a Trunk ports; 2.2.b 802.1Q; 2.2.c Native VLAN.
The chapter also teaches how VLANs break up broadcast domains, how frame tagging works, and how to route between VLANs with a router on a stick and with a Layer 3 switch (SVIs).
Every subnet, mask, broadcast and host range in this chapter (the book's Figures 8.12 to 8.15, my lab addressing, and the review questions) was calculated with a Python
script. All four of the book's worked examples came out correct. The script and its output were run in this session.
What was not done: no command in this document was run on a Cisco switch, router or simulator. Packet Tracer and real IOS behaviour can differ from what is written here.

Book pages 220 to 224. Tracker rows: 8.1, 8.1.1, 8.1.2, 8.1.3. v1.1 objective 2.1. v2.0 objective 2.2.
A switch sends a broadcast out of every port except the one it arrived on. So one switch with no VLANs is one big broadcast domain, however many hosts you plug in. A
(virtual LAN) lets you cut one physical switch into several logical switches. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain. A broadcast sent in VLAN 10 is never sent out of a port that belongs to VLAN 20.
1 per interface (broadcasts are not forwarded by default)
This table is my summary of the book's explanation on pp. 220 to 222
. The book says the same thing in words: switches break up collision domains, routers break up broadcast domains, and VLANs let a switch do the second job at layer 2.
domains. A VLAN (or a router) separates
domains. Examiners like to swap these two.

Four hosts are plugged into one switch. With no VLANs (Figure 8.3) all four receive each other's broadcasts. If you configure Host A and Host B as Sales and Host C and Host D as Admin (Figure 8.4), you get two LANs, two subnets and two broadcast domains on the same physical switch, and you did not buy a second switch. The book says all of these mean the same thing: "two LANs, two subnets, two broadcast domains, two VLANs".
Think of it as a chain:
one VLAN = one broadcast domain = (normally) one IP subnet.
Strictly, a VLAN is layer 2 and a subnet is layer 3, but the book (p. 240) says to give every VLAN its own subnet. Do that.
How VLANs make management easier (the book's list, p. 223).
Adds, moves and changes are easy: you just put the port in the right VLAN.
A group that needs more security can sit in its own VLAN, so outsiders cannot talk to it directly.
VLANs group users by function, not by where they sit.
VLANs greatly improve security if they are implemented correctly (see 8.1.2 for the warning).
VLANs increase the number of broadcast domains and make each one smaller.
Book p. 223. How many broadcasts a network sees depends on three things: the type of protocol, the applications running, and how those services are used.

Multimedia applications use broadcasts and multicasts a lot. Faulty equipment, poor segmentation and badly designed firewalls make it worse. Common broadcasts you already know are ARP requests and DHCP Discover messages.
By default a switch filters broadcasts from every port that is not in the same VLAN as the sender. You get the benefits of a switched network without every user sharing one huge broadcast domain.

Every broadcast interrupts every host in the broadcast domain. Smaller broadcast domains mean less wasted bandwidth and less work for each host's CPU, and a problem in one segment is easier to isolate.

Book pp. 223 to 224. In a flat network the router was supposed to provide security, but that did not work well. Anyone who plugged into the LAN could reach its resources. Anyone could plug a network analyser into a hub and see all traffic. Anyone could join a workgroup just by plugging in.

With VLANs you control each port and which VLAN it is in. Switches can also be set up to tell a network management station about unauthorised access, and you can place restrictions on the router that routes between VLANs.
A VLAN is not a security wall on its own.
The book says VLANs "greatly enhance network security if implemented correctly". The key words are if implemented correctly.

Two classic attacks are switch spoofing (an attacker's PC negotiates a trunk with the switch using DTP) and double tagging (works when the attacker's access VLAN is the same as the trunk's native VLAN). Defences: set every user port to
yourself, do not let user ports negotiate, do not use VLAN 1 or the native VLAN for users, shut unused ports, and filter traffic between VLANs with ACLs or a firewall (Chapter 10).
Source status: general networking knowledge plus Cisco Community statements from Cisco staff. The Cisco VLAN security white paper itself was not opened.
Book p. 224. A layer 2 switch only reads the frame, not the network layer, so by default it floods broadcasts. VLANs create smaller broadcast domains at layer 2.
A broadcast from a node in one VLAN is not forwarded to ports in a different VLAN.
You can add users to a VLAN wherever they are, across one switch or many switches.
A broadcast storm from a faulty NIC stays inside the VLAN where it started. It can still hurt that VLAN.
When a VLAN gets too big, create more VLANs so fewer users are hit by broadcasts.
The book's design tip: keep services local to users where you can, except email and Internet access that everyone needs.
A switch has 12 active ports and no VLANs configured. How many broadcast domains does it have?
B - with no VLANs the whole switch is one broadcast domain. It has 12 collision domains, one per port.
Name two things that split a network into more than one broadcast domain.
VLANs on a switch, and routers (each router interface is a separate broadcast domain) - a plain switch does not do it.
Host A in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request (a broadcast). Which ports receive it?
Only ports in VLAN 10 (access ports in VLAN 10, plus trunks that carry VLAN 10) - ports in other VLANs never see it.
True or false: hosts in two different VLANs on the same switch can talk to each other without a router, because they share the same switch.
False - separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains and subnets. You need a layer 3 device to route between them.

Switch ports are layer 2 interfaces. In this chapter a port is one of two kinds. An
belongs to one VLAN and talks to ordinary devices. A
carries many VLANs at once and talks to other switches, routers or servers that understand VLAN tags. You choose one or the other for each port, not both.

No. It just thinks it is on a LAN.

Devices on an access link cannot reach devices outside their VLAN unless the packet is routed.
In the book's Figure 8.5, two switches are joined by one access link per VLAN (one for Sales, one for Admin). That works, but it uses one port per VLAN on both switches. Trunks fix this.

The word trunk comes from telephone trunks, which carry many calls at once. A trunk port can carry many VLANs at once.
A trunk link is a point-to-point link (100, 1,000, 10,000 Mbps or more) between two switches, a switch and a router, or a switch and a server.

a trunk, only the access VLAN of that port crosses it.
A trunk to a server can put that server in several VLANs at once, so users do not have to cross a router to reach it.

When a frame crosses a trunk, the next switch needs to know which VLAN it belongs to. So the sending switch adds a VLAN ID to the frame. That is

. Each switch reads the VLAN ID from the tag, looks in its filter (forward) table to decide what to do, and removes the tag when the frame leaves through an access port.
(my addition). Host A (VLAN 10) is on SW1 port Fa0/1. Host B (VLAN 10) is on SW2 port Fa0/1. SW1 and SW2 are joined by an 802.1Q trunk.
SW1 assigns the frame to VLAN 10 because of the port's configuration.
SW1 looks up B's MAC address in its VLAN 10 table. The exit port is the trunk.
SW1 inserts the tag and recalculates the frame check sequence.
SW2 reads tag 10 and looks up B in its VLAN 10 table. The exit port is an access port.
SW2 removes the tag. B receives a normal frame.

It is called "on a stick" because a packet from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 goes up the one cable to the router and comes back down the same cable.
Instead of an external router, you create logical interfaces inside a multilayer switch, one per VLAN. They are called switched virtual interfaces (
). The routing happens on the switch backplane, which is faster and more efficient than an external router.

The book says router on a stick "is what's used on the CCNA objectives for inter-VLAN routing". In v1.1 the objective is 2.1.c "InterVLAN connectivity" (the book's v1.0 text says just "Connectivity"). In the official v2.0 PDF the phrase "router on a stick" does not appear. v2.0 lists switch-to-router connectivity (2.1), 802.1Q trunk interfaces (2.1.b) and the SVI (2.1.d). Learn both ROAS and SVI.

On pp. 229 to 231 the book discusses 2600, 2800 and 3560 models, FastEthernet interfaces and the price of used equipment. Ignore the model advice. It is not exam content, and the 2600 and 2800 are end-of-life. What matters is the design idea.
Which inter-VLAN routing method uses subinterfaces?
Router on a stick - one physical interface is split into one subinterface per VLAN.
Why is router on a stick a single point of failure and a bottleneck?
All inter-VLAN traffic goes through one router interface and one cable - if either fails, no VLAN can reach another VLAN.
In a router-on-a-stick design, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 20?
The IP address of the router subinterface that handles VLAN 20 - not the physical interface address.

Defining the allowed VLANs on a trunk
Book pp. 238 to 239. A trunk allows every VLAN by default. You can remove VLANs from the allowed list to stop their traffic crossing that link.

S1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan all
takes a range out of the current list. Use a hyphen for a range.

A switch has 12 access ports in use, spread over 3 VLANs. How many collision domains and broadcast domains does it have?
12 collision domains and 3 broadcast domains - one collision domain per port, one broadcast domain per VLAN.
Which port type sends and receives frames without a VLAN tag?
B - an access port sends untagged frames.
How many bytes does an 802.1Q tag add to a frame?
B - 4 bytes. 26 and 30 relate to ISL.
How many VLANs can the 802.1Q VLAN ID identify, and why?
4,094 (1 to 4094) - 12 bits gives 4,096 values; 0 and 4,095 are reserved.
Which VLAN IDs are the normal range on Cisco switches, and which are reserved within it?
1 to 1005, where 1002 to 1005 are reserved (and VLAN 1 is the default) - extended range is 1006 to 4094.
Which VLAN carries untagged frames on an 802.1Q trunk by default?
B - the native VLAN, VLAN 1 by default.

switchport voice vlan 30 - the PC stays in the access VLAN.
